info.title: The Clinical and Cellular Landscape of DKK1 in Osteosarcoma

text.text: Dickkopf-1 (DKK1) is a secreted protein that acts as a Wnt antagonist and is implicated in osteosarcoma progression.
Elevated circulating DKK1 levels have been described at OS diagnosis, but its circulating dynamics, prognostic relevance, and cellular distribution remain incompletely characterized.

We analysed longitudinal plasma DKK1 in 34 patients using mixed-effects models, evaluated DKK1 expression and survival in two independent transcriptomic cohorts, and examined cellular and tissue distribution using single-cell transcriptomics and immunohistochemistry.
Cultured mesenchymal stem cells were assessed as potential nonmalignant sources.
Circulating DKK1 declined by 12.4% per 30-day period during treatment, without significant changes detected around primary tumour resection or relapse.
Metastatic presentation and poor histologic response were associated with higher estimated DKK1 levels.
Higher tumour DKK1 expression was associated with worse overall and metastasis-free survival (pooled HRs per SD increase: 1.35 [95% CI 1.02-1.78] and 1.48 [1.06-2.07], respectively).
DKK1 transcripts were predominantly detected in malignant cells across multiple subpopulations and protein staining was enriched in osteoid and matrix-rich regions of primary tumours.
Tumour DKK1 expression is associated with adverse outcomes, while circulating concentration decline over treatment time.
These findings support further prognostic evaluation and investigation of the associations among DKK1 expression and production, tissue localisation, and circulating levels.
One of the central challenges in the treatment of osteosarcoma (OS) is metastatic progression.

Although the combination of surgery and multi-agent chemotherapy results in long-term survival in approximately 70% of patients with localized disease, outcomes remain poor for patients with metastatic or recurrent OS [1].

text.text: Attempts to intensify conventional chemotherapy have failed to improve outcomes, while many clinical trials investigating systemic therapies for recurrent disease have likewise yielded limited benefits [2, 3].

text.text: These limitations highlight the need to identify molecular pathways involved in metastatic progression, particularly those that may be therapeutically targeted or evaluated through circulating biomarkers.

text.text: Together, these findings implicate DKK1 in tumour progression and suggest that its effects on osteogenic differentiation and bone homeostasis may contribute to interactions between tumour cells and their surrounding microenvironment.
As a secreted protein, DKK1 is also detectable in circulation.
Newly diagnosed OS presents with elevated serum DKK1 compared to healthy controls, suggesting potential utility as a biomarker [15].

text.text: This provides a rationale for evaluating circulating DKK1 in OS patients longitudinally to understand whether circulating DKK1 concentrations change during treatment, reflect disease burden, or correlate with clinical characteristics.
In this study, we quantified plasma DKK1 concentrations during OS treatment and follow-up and assessed associations with metastatic presentation and histologic response.
We then evaluated the relationships between DKK1 expression in biopsy samples with patient outcomes in two public OS cohorts.

Finally, we integrated single-cell transcriptomic analyses with immunohistochemical staining of patient tumour specimens to characterize the cellular distribution of DKK1 and identify candidate cell populations involved in its signalling.

Together, these analyses aimed to characterize the dynamics of circulating DKK1, evaluate the prognostic relevance of tumour DKK1 expression, and investigate its cellular distribution and potential signalling context within the OS microenvironment.

Given the heterogeneous distribution of DKK1 transcript across malignant cell states, and the possibility that secreted DKK1 protein may accumulate at sites far from its cellular site of production, we decided to explore protein expression in primary tumour samples.
We performed immunohistochemical staining of DKK1 on a tissue microarray (TMA) containing 50 cores from primary OS tumours.

Using QuPath, we developed a pathologist-guided pixel classifier to distinguish three histologic tumour compartments: matrix-poor/cell dense regions, matrix-rich tumour regions, and osteoid (Fig. 4C).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that, although DKK1 transcripts are detected predominantly in malignant cells, DKK1 protein expression is preferentially distributed within osteoid and matrix-rich regions of primary tumours.
Given the association between tumoral DKK1 expression and metastatic hazard, we next investigated whether circulating DKK1 changed upon disease relapse.
Plasma DKK1 concentrations were higher at relapse compared with end-of-therapy samples, although this was not statistically significant (Fig. 5A).

text.text: As relapse occurred at different timepoints during treatment or follow-up across patients, we compared each patient's relapse sample with their most recent available pre-relapse sample (Fig. 5B).

text.text: This paired analysis revealed no significant change in circulating DKK1 at relapse, consistent with our finding that circulating DKK1 does not behave like a real-time readout of tumour burden.

Finally, given the potential contribution of nonmalignant cells to circulating DKK1, particularly at the time of relapse, we explored whether DKK1 expression could be associated with a reactive stromal phenotype.

We analysed transcriptomic data from primary osteoblasts and human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stem cells (ucMSCs) cultured under basal conditions, induced towards osteogenic differentiation, or cultured in conditioned medium from control or TGF-β-overexpressing LNCaP cells to promote a reactive, myofibroblast-like phenotype.
DKK1 expression was elevated in the TGF-β-exposed ucMSCs compared with other conditions (Fig. 5C).
text.formatted: DKK1 expression was elevated in the TGF-β-exposed ucMSCs compared with other conditions (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5C</ref>).

text.text: This suggests that DKK1 expression may be associated with TGF-β-induced MSC activation, identifying a potential nonmalignant source that could augment the DKK1 levels that derive from the malignant tumour cells.
Circulating DKK1 declines over treatment course, with no noticeable abrupt change around the time of surgical resection of the primary tumour.
Previous studies have shown elevated DKK1 serum levels at diagnosis in OS patients, as well as protein expression in the tumour [15].
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown elevated DKK1 serum levels at diagnosis in OS patients, as well as protein expression in the tumour <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: These findings extend earlier cross-sectional observations of elevated serum DKK1 in OS by characterizing its trajectory during treatment.
We also show that higher diagnostic tumour DKK1 expression is associated with poorer survival outcomes and with increased metastatic risk.

Our analysis of single-cell transcriptomic datasets show that DKK1 transcripts are predominantly attributable to malignant cells within primary tumours, with the protein being enriched in matrix-rich and osteoid compartments of the tumour.

Taken together, these observations suggest a unique role of DKK1 at the interface between malignant-cell biology and the surrounding bone and stromal environment, although the separate study cohorts prevent direct assessment of how tumour expression and tissue localization relate to circulating concentrations.
The main finding that DKK1 levels decline monotonically during treatment raises the possibility of multiple potential DKK1 sources.

Chemotherapy-induced cell death likely plays a role in this reduction, as the decline in DKK1 precedes surgical resection of the tumour, while host responses to the tumour, treatment, and tissue repair may influence subsequent concentrations.
In addition, the resection itself does not seemingly alter the course of the decline, which is compatible with an additional, nonmalignant source of circulating DKK1.

Recent work in bone-metastatic breast cancer models has shown that bone-derived DKK1 is the predominant source of systemic DKK1, while cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) contribute most of the tumoral DKK1 in the primary lesion [17].

text.text: In OS, reactive changes in the surrounding bone and postoperative repair are therefore plausible contributors.
Platelets are another likely nonmalignant source, as it has been shown that DKK1 protein is present in platelet extracts [16, 22].

text.text: Interestingly, DKK1 mRNA is not expressed in platelets, suggesting that DKK1 protein presence in platelets is due to uptake by endocytosis [22].
text.formatted: Interestingly, DKK1 mRNA is not expressed in platelets, suggesting that DKK1 protein presence in platelets is due to uptake by endocytosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, platelets may provide a releasable pool of DKK1 without identifying the tissue in which the protein was originally synthesized.

We also explored the relationship between tumour DKK1 expression and patient survival, and show that a continuous expression analysis supports a negative association between DKK1 and both overall survival and relapse-free/metastasis-free survival.
Notably, there is evidence that DKK1-targeted therapy reduces ALDH activity, enhances osteogenic differentiation in the primary tumour, reduces metastatic burden in OS models [11] [12] [13] 23].

text.text: Wnt inhibition through DKK1 expression has also been shown to promote a quiescent, immune-evading state in lung and breast cancer models, suggesting that DKK1 can influence persistence and immune escape, which are critical for the establishment of a metastatic niche [24].

text.text: An additional finding of this study was the potential relationship between circulating DKK1 and histologic response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
DKK1 concentrations at diagnosis were not significantly associated with subsequent tumour necrosis, suggesting that baseline DKK1 alone is not a predictor of histologic response.
However, when longitudinal measurements were considered, patients with good histologic response had lower adjusted DKK1 concentrations throughout treatment, albeit with some uncertainty.

These findings raise the possibility that changes in circulating DKK1 during neoadjuvant chemotherapy may be more informative about treatment-associated biological responses than its concentration at diagnosis.
Experimental work linking DKK1 to ALDH-associated stress-tolerance provides a biological rationale for examining the relationship of DKK1 to chemoresistance [23].
text.formatted: Experimental work linking DKK1 to ALDH-associated stress-tolerance provides a biological rationale for examining the relationship of DKK1 to chemoresistance <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Larger prospective cohorts with serial sampling and detailed histologic response data will be required to determine whether early changes in DKK1 provide information about chemotherapy response beyond baseline measurements.
DKK1 expression across several malignant cell states suggests that it is not restricted to a single differentiation programme.

This finding fits with recent studies showing that OS comprises heterogeneous mesenchymal and osteoblast-associated states that can coexist within individual tumours, with subpopulations existing along multiple potential mesenchymal lineages [25, 26].
text.formatted: This finding fits with recent studies showing that OS comprises heterogeneous mesenchymal and osteoblast-associated states that can coexist within individual tumours, with subpopulations existing along multiple potential mesenchymal lineages <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26]</ref>.

text.text: Our analysis of scRNA-seq datasets show both progenitor-like tumour cells and more differentiated matrix-associated tumour cells express DKK1.

Earlier work has also shown that DKK1 is regulated by the osteoblast transcription factor Sp7, while DKK1 immunodepletion attenuates the inhibition of osteogenesis in MSCs cultured in OS-conditioned medium [9, 15].
text.formatted: Earlier work has also shown that DKK1 is regulated by the osteoblast transcription factor Sp7, while DKK1 immunodepletion attenuates the inhibition of osteogenesis in MSCs cultured in OS-conditioned medium <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: Osteoid production, thus, need not imply completion of terminal osteogenic differentiation, and DKK1 may participate in paracrine regulation within a heterogeneous tumour.
These possibilities require functional testing, particularly as the consequences of Wnt signalling repression differ across OS models [27, 28].
text.formatted: These possibilities require functional testing, particularly as the consequences of Wnt signalling repression differ across OS models <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>.

text.text: Our IHC analysis shows a clear enrichment of DKK1 protein along matrix-rich and osteoid regions of the tumour, adding a spatial dimension to this interpretation.
Importantly, protein localization need not coincide with the site of transcription, as secretion, extracellular association, and turnover can influence local availability.
This could point to the osteoid matrix being a DKK1 reservoir, and DKK1-glycosaminoglycan interactions have been identified, showing this extracellular association is plausible [29].
text.formatted: This could point to the osteoid matrix being a DKK1 reservoir, and DKK1-glycosaminoglycan interactions have been identified, showing this extracellular association is plausible <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: The discordance between cellular transcript expression and extracellular protein distribution also raises the possibility that OS cells produce DKK1 to modulate differentiation within the tumour environment.
However, our staining does not establish a functional reservoir or identify the cells that produce or respond to the protein.
Combined spatial transcriptomics and histological DKK1 staining could be used to assess these hypotheses, and would allow us to deconvolute candidate DKK1 sources and protein localization.

In addition, spatial transcriptomic analysis could reveal receptor localization and downstream pathway readouts, allowing us to distinguish production from accumulation and identify candidate paracrine relationships.
Recent spatial transcriptomic studies in OS demonstrate the feasibility of this approach [30].
text.formatted: Recent spatial transcriptomic studies in OS demonstrate the feasibility of this approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Our observation of increased DKK1 expression in MSCs treated with cultured media from TGF-βoverexpressing LNCaP cells provides another link between potential host sources of DKK1 and tumour-associated tissue responses.
TGF-β signalling is a mediator of wound response stromal remodelling and has been shown to induce a fibrotic response in mesenchymal stem cells, including lung-resident MSCs [31] [32] [33].
text.formatted: TGF-β signalling is a mediator of wound response stromal remodelling and has been shown to induce a fibrotic response in mesenchymal stem cells, including lung-resident MSCs <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, the response of MSCs to TGF-β stimulation in the context of the profibrotic microenvironment could be associated with pulmonary metastatic colonization.

Notably, recent work has shown that disseminated OS cells induce a persistent wound-healing response in the lung, accompanied by profibrotic epithelial and macrophage states as well as extensive ECM deposition [34].
text.formatted: Notably, recent work has shown that disseminated OS cells induce a persistent wound-healing response in the lung, accompanied by profibrotic epithelial and macrophage states as well as extensive ECM deposition <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, our results raise the possibility that mesenchymal cells responding to tissue injury or profibrotic signals in the lung might provide an additional source of DKK1.
This possibility informs our working model (Fig. 5D), in which DKK1 production and local availability reflect contributions from tumour cells and responsive host compartments.
text.formatted: This possibility informs our working model (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5D</ref>), in which DKK1 production and local availability reflect contributions from tumour cells and responsive host compartments.

text.text: Such contributions could help explain why circulating concentrations do not change directly with removal of the primary tumour.
However, whether analogous DKK1-producing mesenchymal states occur within pulmonary metastatic niches and whether their DKK1 contributes to circulating levels remains to be established.
Our findings have different implications for biomarker development and prognostics.
The association between DKK1 expression and adverse outcomes supports further evaluation of DKK1 as a prognostic marker.

In contrast, plasma DKK1 does not behave like a real-time readout of tumour burden, so its utility for monitoring tumour burden or chemotherapy response, or for detecting disease progression, remains uncertain.
Prospective studies should evaluate whether early changes in plasma DKK1 improve assessment of treatment response.
The associations presented here also complement existing preclinical evidence that DKK1targeted interventions can reduce OS progression and metastasis [11] [12] [13].
text.formatted: The associations presented here also complement existing preclinical evidence that DKK1targeted interventions can reduce OS progression and metastasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Receptor context may be important to this approach, because DKK1 can activate CKAP4-dependent PI3K signalling as well as antagonize canonical Wnt signalling [35].
text.formatted: Receptor context may be important to this approach, because DKK1 can activate CKAP4-dependent PI3K signalling as well as antagonize canonical Wnt signalling <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: These findings provide a rationale for further therapeutic investigation; receptor expression and downstream pathway activity may clarify the biological consequences of DKK1 inhibition.
Several limitations constrain the interpretation of the plasma DKK1 findings.
Although repeated sampling allowed assessment of within-patient changes, the total number of patients was modest, particularly those with metastatic disease at diagnosis.
In addition, missing histologicresponse data reduced the multivariable analysis cohort.
Associations with metastatic disease and tumour necrosis thus require confirmation with larger sample sizes.

Surgery dates were not available for analysis, so they were estimated using the post-surgical sample draw dates, so it is possible that immediate abrupt changes in DKK1 occurring post-operatively were missed.

Furthermore, the plasma, bulk transcriptomic, single-cell transcriptomic, and histological analyses involved separate cohorts, preventing direct assessment of how tumoral DKK1 expression and protein localization relate to circulating concentrations in individual patients.
Bulk expression may reflect cellular composition as well as expression within individual cells, while single-cell estimates depend on cell recovery, transcript detection, and annotation.
This is particularly important for DKK1, whose expression may be low and transient.
Likewise, expression in cultured mesenchymal cells demonstrates a potential source under the tested conditions but does not quantify its contribution in patients.

Paired longitudinal sampling, spatial RNA-protein analysis, and functional perturbation will be needed to test the proposed relationships among DKK1 production, extracellular localization, and tumour-host signalling.

Cell classifications were obtained from the original OsteoCAR annotations, using Level 0 to distinguish malignant tumour cells from nonmalignant host cells and Level 2 to identify specific cell populations and malignant transcriptional states.
Raw transcript counts were extracted from the Seurat RNA assay.
DKK1 counts were summed across cells belonging to each Level 2 population to generate per-sample cell-state-level pseudobulk counts.
The relative contribution of each population was calculated by dividing its summed DKK1 counts by the total DKK1 counts detected across all malignant and nonmalignant cells from the same specimen.
Specimens with no detected DKK1 transcripts were assigned undefined rather than zero source fractions.
For comparisons of DKK1 expression between specimens, raw counts from malignant cells were summed by gene within each specimen to generate sample-level pseudobulk profiles.

DKK1 expression was normalized to counts per million (CPM), using the total number of transcripts detected across all genes in the malignant compartment as the denominator, and transformed as log₂(CPM + 1).
The proportion of DKK1-expressing cells was assessed using log-normalized RNA expression data.
Cells with detectable DKK1 expression (DKK1 > 0) were classified as DKK1-positive, corresponding to nonzero raw DKK1 counts.

Sections were incubated overnight in primary antibody at 4 °C (Bioss Inc., BS2162R 1:200) diluted in primary antibody diluent (GeneTex, GTX28208).

An area-weighted staining score (range, 0-300) was calculated by summing the three cumulative positive-area percentages.

Induction of myofibroblast phenotype Cells were seeded in plastic 6-well plates (Fisher, #FB012927) at 50,000 cells per well and allowed to adhere overnight.

For collection, media was removed from the wells, and 100 microliters of RLT Buffer (Qiagen) was added per well.

RNA was then purified using the Qiagen RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen, #74106), according to the manufacturer's instructions.
RNA-seq library construction and sequencing for two technical replicates was carried out by Genewiz/Azenta (South Plainfield, NJ).
Sequence reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic v.0.36. trimmed reads were mapped to the Homo Sapiens GRCh37 reference genome using STAR aligner v.2.5.2b.

text.text: Statistical analyses were performed in R 4.4.3.
Longitudinal changes in log₁₀-transformed plasma DKK1 were assessed using linear mixed-effects models, incorporating patient-specific random intercepts to account for repeated measurements.

The primary model, for the interval between diagnosis and end of therapy, included days from diagnosis, age, metastatic status at diagnosis, histologic response, and Luminex assay plate as fixed effects.
Model coefficients were back-transformed to express adjusted concentration ratios.

Concentrations below the assay's lower limit of detection (150 pg/mL; 26 of 210 patient samples) were set to half the limit (75 pg/mL) before log transformation; alternative substitutions are shown in Supp.
Fig. 1F.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1F</ref>.

text.text: Models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and tbased 95% confidence intervals.
All available samples were used in the mixed models, including repeated pre-local-control draws; paired comparisons used the latest sample at each stage.

Nonlinear changes across the complete follow-up period were evaluated using generalized additive mixed models, incorporating a cubic regression spline for time, assay plate, and a patient-specific random effect.
Changes around local control were assessed using mixed-effects models with treatment stage as a categorical predictor.
Within-patient changes between diagnosis and subsequent treatment stages were assessed using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, with Hodges-Lehmann estimates and 95% confidence intervals.
An exact binomial sign test was additionally used to evaluate the direction of change before local control.
Pre-versus post-surgical samples were compared with paired t-tests on log10 concentrations.
Relationships between plasma DKK1 and percent tumour necrosis were examined using Spearman rank correlations, and comparisons between histologic response groups used Wilcoxon rank-sum tests.
Differences in DKK1 immunoreactivity across tissue compartments were assessed using Friedman tests followed by pairwise Conover tests.
P values were adjusted using the Holm procedure for specified pairwise comparisons and the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure for geneset analyses.
All tests were two-sided, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant.
